excerpt: The NCERT Class 6 Decimals chapter trips up a lot of students at the tenths-and-hundredths stage. Here is the chapter explained in plain language, with two worked case studies and a quick quiz to check understanding.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 6 student the numbers 0.7 and 0.35 and ask which is bigger, and a surprising number will pick 0.35 — because 35 looks larger than 7. That single mistake tells you almost everything about why the class 6 maths decimals chapter matters. A decimal is not a whole number with a dot dropped in; it is a new way of writing parts of one, and the place a digit sits in decides its value. Get that idea right and the rest of the NCERT chapter — reading, comparing, converting and calculating — falls into place.

I have taught this chapter to plenty of Tier-2 city students who arrived shaky on fractions, and the pattern is always the same: the ones who slow down over place value sail through everything after it. So that is where we start.

Decimal place value: tenths, hundredths and thousandths

To the right of the decimal point, each place is ten times smaller than the one before it. The first place is tenths (one whole cut into 10 equal parts), the second is hundredths (cut into 100), the third is thousandths (cut into 1000). So in 4.286 the 2 means 2 tenths, the 8 means 8 hundredths, and the 6 means 6 thousandths.

Now the 0.7 versus 0.35 question answers itself. 0.7 is 7 tenths, which is the same as 70 hundredths; 0.35 is only 35 hundredths. Seventy beats thirty-five. The counter-intuitive bit — that a shorter decimal can be the larger one — is exactly the insight the chapter is built to fix.

Reading and comparing decimals

Read 4.286 as ‘four point two eight six’, not ‘four point two hundred eighty-six’. After the point you name the digits one by one, because each sits in its own place. To compare two decimals, line up the decimal points and compare place by place from the left, and give the shorter number trailing zeros so both have the same number of decimal places.

  • Compare the ones digits first; the bigger one wins outright.
  • If they tie, move to tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
  • Adding trailing zeros never changes the value: 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700.

So to compare 3.4 and 3.38, write 3.4 as 3.40. Tenths: 4 beats 3, so 3.4 is larger. That trick of padding with zeros removes almost every comparison error I see.

Converting fractions to decimals and back

Fractions with 10, 100 or 1000 on the bottom convert straight away, because those are exactly the decimal places. Seven-tenths is 0.7. Twenty-three hundredths is 0.23. Going the other way, read the last place to find the denominator: 0.9 is 9/10, and 0.45 is 45/100, which simplifies to 9/20.

When the denominator is not 10, 100 or 1000

Turn it into one that is. One-half becomes 5/10 = 0.5 (multiply top and bottom by 5). Three-quarters becomes 75/100 = 0.75. This is the NCERT way, and it keeps the reasoning visible instead of hiding it inside long division too early.

Adding and subtracting decimals in money and length

The whole point of decimals in Class 6 is that they describe real quantities — rupees and paise, metres and centimetres, kilograms and grams. To add or subtract, line up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths, fill gaps with zeros, then add or subtract as usual and bring the point straight down.

Case study 1: the stationery bill

Riya buys a notebook for ₹42.50, a pen for ₹15.75 and a geometry box for ₹89.00. She hands the shopkeeper a ₹200 note. How much does she spend, and what change does she get?

Add the prices, points aligned: 42.50 + 15.75 + 89.00 = ₹147.25. Change from ₹200 is 200.00 − 147.25 = ₹52.75. Notice how paise are just hundredths of a rupee — ₹42.50 is forty-two rupees and fifty paise, or 42 and 50 hundredths. Money is the friendliest place to meet hundredths, because students already live in it.

Case study 2: the ribbon

A tailor has 5 m of ribbon. She cuts one piece of 1.35 m and another of 2.4 m. How much ribbon is left? First make the lengths match: 2.4 m is 2.40 m. Used ribbon is 1.35 + 2.40 = 3.75 m. Left over is 5.00 − 3.75 = 1.25 m. Because 1 m is 100 cm, 1.25 m is the same as 125 cm — a neat check that reading across units is just reading across decimal places.

This is exactly how the case-study e-book below is built: a short real-life passage, then questions that force you to pick the right operation rather than just crunch numbers you were handed.

Common slip-ups worth naming

  • Treating 0.5 and 0.05 as equal — the extra zero pushes the 5 into hundredths, making it ten times smaller.
  • Adding without aligning the points, so 4.5 + 0.75 turns into nonsense.
  • Forgetting that ₹7.5 and ₹7.50 are the same amount, seven rupees fifty paise.

One honest caveat: do not rush a child onto decimal multiplication and division, which come later. Class 6 asks for solid place value, confident comparing, clean conversion, and careful addition and subtraction. Nail those four and the harder operations become almost boring — in the best way.

questions.q: In the number 4.286, what does the digit 8 represent?
questions.explanation: The second place after the point is hundredths, so the 8 in 4.286 means 8 hundredths.
0.7 is 70 hundredths, which is more than 35, 68 or 40.9 hundredths. A shorter decimal can still be the biggest.
3/4 = 75/100 = 0.75 after multiplying top and bottom by 25.

questions.q: What is 0.45 written as a fraction in simplest form?
Riya spends ₹42.50 and ₹15.75. How much is that altogether?
Which of these is equal to 0.5?
questions.explanation: Adding a trailing zero does not change the value, so 0.5 = 0.50. But 0.05 is ten times smaller.

questions.q: A ribbon of 5 m has 3.75 m used. How much is left?
How many centimetres are there in 1.25 m?
questions.explanation: 1 m is 100 cm, so 1.25 m is 125 cm. Moving across units matches moving across decimal places.

faq.q: What topics are in the Class 6 NCERT Decimals chapter?
faq.a: It covers decimal place value (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), reading and comparing decimals, converting between fractions and decimals, and adding and subtracting decimals in money and measurement contexts.

faq.q: Why do students think 0.35 is bigger than 0.7?
faq.a: They compare 35 against 7 as whole numbers and ignore place value. 0.7 is 70 hundredths while 0.35 is only 35 hundredths, so 0.7 is larger. Padding the shorter number with a zero — 0.7 becomes 0.70 — makes the comparison obvious.

faq.q: How do you turn a fraction into a decimal in Class 6?
faq.a: Rewrite the fraction so its denominator is 10, 100 or 1000, then read it straight off. For example, 3/4 becomes 75/100 = 0.75, and 1/2 becomes 5/10 = 0.5.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when adding decimals?
faq.a: Not lining up the decimal points. Always stack tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths, fill any gaps with zeros, then add and bring the point straight down.
